{{Short description|Professor}}
[[Image:Edme Pourchot.jpg|thumb|right|100px|Edmond Pourchot.]]
'''Edmond Pourchot''' (1651, [[Poilly]] – 1734, [[Paris]])  was a university professor noted for his controversial advocacy of [[Cartesianism]] (and the [[Cartesian physics|Cartesian]] theory of [[classical mechanics|mechanics]]) in place of [[Aristotelianism]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.scholasticon.fr/Database/Scholastiques_fr.php?ID=1040 |title=Pourchot, Edmond - Scholasticon |access-date=2010-05-29 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716060633/http://www.scholasticon.fr/Database/Scholastiques_fr.php?ID=1040 |archive-date=2011-07-16 }}</ref><ref>'''Watt, R.''' ''Bibliotheca Britannica; Or a General Index to British and Foreign Literature.'' [[Edinburgh]], 1824.</ref> The change within the [[University of Paris]] from Aristotelianism to Cartesianism during the 1690s was important in the history of the development of [[natural philosophy]] in [[France]] and continental [[Europe]].<ref>'''Brockliss, Laurence.''' ''The Moment of No Return: The University of Paris and the Death of Aristotelianism.'' Science & Education, March 2006, pp259-278.</ref><ref>'''Santinello, G. & G. Piaia.''' ''Models of the History of Philosophy.'' Springer, 2011.</ref>

Pourchot was named Professor of Philosophy in 1677, and he was a long-standing vice-chancellor/rector of the University of Paris, where he taught for 26 years. He authored a popular multi-volume [[Latin]] text entitled ''Institutiones philosophicae ad faciliorem veterum, ac recentiorum philosophorum lectionem comparatae'' (Paris, 1695; Paris, 1700; [[Lyon]], 1711; [[Venice]], 1715; Lyon, 1716–1717; Venice, 1730 [standard edition]; Paris & Lyon & [[Padua]], 1733; Padua, 1751; Venice, 1755).<ref>Dates and places of publication from Heritage of the Printed Book database, COPAC, and BnF catalogues.</ref><ref>[[:it:Edmond Pourchot]]</ref> This text was well regarded among other French intellectuals, and gained followers for Cartesianism in many other countries including [[Turkey]] and [[Poland]].<ref>''Chalmer's Biography'', 1812, vol 25, p239.</ref><ref>'''Shaw, S.J.''' ''History of the Ottoman Empire and Modern Turkey.'' Cambridge University Press, 1976.</ref> He was also a scholar of the [[Hebrew language]]. The Latin form of his name was '''Edmundus Purchotius''' ('''Edmundi Purchotii''').
[[Image:Pourchot-001.jpg|thumb|right|100px|''Institutiones Philosophicae'' (1717).]]
* Volume 1<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-1c-AAAAYAAJ&q=(pourchot+OR+purchotius+OR+purchotii)+AND+institutiones|title=Institutiones philosophicae ad faciliorem veterum|last1=Pourchot|first1=Edme|year=1711}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=iyN-7Z2yd4wC&q=edmond+pourchot+institutiones+philosophicae&pg=RA1-PT357|title=Institutiones philosophicae ad faciliorem veterum ac recentiorum ...|last1=Pourchot|first1=Edmond|year=1711}}</ref> - [[Logic]] and [[metaphysics]]
* Volume 2<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fvphNdUMqAgC&q=(pourchot+OR+Purchotius+OR+Purchotii)+AND+institutiones|title=Institutiones philosophicae ad faciliorem veterum, ac recentiorum ...|last1=Pourchot|first1=Edmond|year=1751}}</ref> - [[Geometry]] and general [[physics]] (including [[optics]], [[hydrodynamics]], [[simple machine]]s, [[thermodynamics]], and [[dynamics (physics)|dynamics]] featuring [[projectile]]s, [[pendulum]]s, etc.)
* Volume 3<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ie8GAAAAcAAJ&q=(pourchot+OR+purchotius+OR+purchotii)+AND+institutiones&pg=PP7|title=Institutiones philosophicae|last1=Pourchot|first1=Edmond|year=1751}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wfMGAAAAcAAJ&q=edmond+pourchot+institutiones+philosophicae&pg=PA501|title=Institutiones Philosophicae|last1=Pourchot|first1=Edmond|year=1711}}</ref> - [[Cosmology]] ([[heliocentric]] and [[geocentric]]), [[botany]], [[zoology]], [[human anatomy]], [[meteorology]], [[astronomy]], [[magnetism]], [[metallurgy]], and [[geography]]
:# including a world map showing [[Terra Australis]], the [[Prime Meridian]] passing through [[El Hierro]], and the [[Island of California]] (Table 24)
:# including a presentation of heliocentric Cartesian [[Mechanical explanations of gravitation|ethereal vortices]] in/around the [[Solar System]] (Table 20)...<ref>{{cite book|url=https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/descartes-physics/|title=Descartes' Physics|publisher=Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University|year=2017}}</ref> this theory was supported by many notable scientists (for example [[Christiaan Huygens]] and [[Johann Bernoulli]]) prior to being supplanted by [[Isaac Newton|Newtonian]] mechanics (published 1686)<ref>'''Lakatos, Imre.''' ''The Methodology of Scientific Research Programmes.'' Cambridge University Press, 1978.</ref><ref>'''Solomon, Joan.''' ''The Structure of Space.'' Wiley, 1974.</ref>
:# including an [[armillary sphere]] showing the plane of the [[ecliptic]] on the [[celestial sphere]] (Table 16)
:# including an illustration of magnetic [[field line]]s which were not fully understood for another 150 years until [[Michael Faraday|Faraday]] and [[James Clerk Maxwell|Maxwell]] (Table 26)
* Volume 4<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=avP0BciesggC&q=(pourchot+OR+purchotius+OR+purchotii)+AND+institutiones|title=Institutiones philosophicae, 1|last1=Pourchot|first1=Edme|year=1715}}</ref> - [[Ethics]]
* Volume 5<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=wvAGAAAAcAAJ&q=(pourchot+OR+purchotius+OR+purchotii)+AND+institutiones|title=Institutiones Philosophicae|year=1760|last1=Pourchot|first1=Edmond}}</ref> - [[Philosophy]] (including [[metaphysics]] and [[ontology]])
